analysis.evidence: The singular verb agrees with הַנָּחָשׁ, the serpent. אֶל הָאִשָּׁה identifies the woman as the addressee, and לֹא מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן gives the serpent’s words.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר הַנָּחָשׁ אֶל־הָאִשָּׁה, “the serpent said to the woman,” הַנָּחָשׁ is the subject of וַיֹּאמֶר. The definite article identifies the serpent already speaking with the woman.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר הַנָּחָשׁ אֶל הָאִשָּׁה, “the serpent said to the woman,” אֶל introduces the woman as the addressee.
In וַיֹּאמֶר הַנָּחָשׁ אֶל הָאִשָּׁה, “the serpent said to the woman,” the phrase אֶל הָאִשָּׁה identifies the woman as the addressee.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute common noun with the definite article הָ־.

analysis.evidence: In לֹא מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן, לֹא negates the death prediction emphasized by the infinitive absolute מוֹת. The serpent tells the woman, “You will certainly not die.”
analysis.morphology: Negative particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: מוֹת precedes תְּמֻתוּן, a finite verb from the same root. The infinitive absolute adds emphasis under לֹא, giving the serpent’s denial the force of “you will surely not die.”
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive absolute, with no prefix or suffix

analysis.evidence: תְּמֻתוּן is the finite verb. The preceding infinitive absolute מוֹת adds emphasis, and לֹא negates the statement. The serpent tells the woman, “You will certainly not die,” using a plural “you.”
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine plural, with final paragogic nun
analysis.sense: die, come to the end of life
